paraphrase: Whereas some ascetics and brahmins, living on food given in faith, make their living by wrong livelihood through such low arts (tiracchāna-vijjā) as reading limbs, omens, portents and dreams; marks of gems, weapons, persons and animals; predicting the marches and victories of kings; predicting eclipses of moon, sun and asterisms, their right and wrong courses, meteors, sky-glow, earthquakes and thunder, and their results; forecasting rain, harvest, safety and disease; fixing auspicious days for marriages; and pacificatory and propitiatory rites — the ascetic Gotama refrains from such low arts and wrong livelihood.

paraphrase: (The low arts include predicting:) 'there will be an eclipse of the moon, of the sun, of an asterism; the moon and sun will go on their course or off it; the asterisms will go on or off course; there will be a meteor, sky-glow, earthquake, thunder; the rising and setting, darkening and brightening of moon, sun and asterisms — and such will be the result of each.'

paraphrase: Eternalism (sassatavāda) on four grounds: some ascetics and brahmins, by ardent effort and right attention, reach a concentration in which they recall up to a hundred thousand past lives, or ten, or forty aeons of contraction and expansion, and conclude that self and world are eternal, barren, firm as a pillar, while beings transmigrate; the fourth kind reaches the same conclusion by reasoning. The Tathāgata knows where such grounds lead in the next life, knows what is beyond them, and is freed by not grasping.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha's catalogue of the views of 'some ascetics and brahmins' (DN 1, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: Ascetics and brahmins who theorise about the past and the future do so on sixty-two grounds: eternalism, partial eternalism, the world as finite or infinite, evasive 'eel-wriggling', chance origination (eighteen about the past); the self after death as percipient, non-percipient or neither, annihilationism, and nibbāna here and now identified with sense-pleasure or the jhānas (forty-four about the future).

paraphrase: If others speak against the Buddha, the teaching or the Saṅgha, the monks should not be angry or displeased, nor elated if others praise them; they should explain what is untrue as untrue, or acknowledge what is true as true.

paraphrase: When an ordinary person praises the Tathāgata, it is only for trifling matters of mere virtue — abstaining from killing, stealing, unchastity, false and harsh speech, and from the many kinds of low arts, divination and luxury listed in the short, middle and long sections on virtue.

paraphrase: Partial eternalism (ekacca-sassatavāda) on four grounds: (1) the being first reborn in an empty Brahmā-palace after the world's contraction thinks 'I am Brahmā, the maker, the creator, the father of beings', and later beings agree; one who falls from there and recalls it holds Brahmā permanent and himself impermanent; (2) gods corrupted by play (khiḍḍā-padosika) and (3) gods corrupted by mind (mano-padosika) fall from their state and judge the others permanent; (4) the reasoner holds eye, ear, nose, tongue and body an impermanent self, but mind or consciousness a permanent self.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha's catalogue of the views of 'some ascetics and brahmins' (DN 1, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: Views that the world is finite or infinite (antānantika) on four grounds: in meditation some perceive the world as finite, others as infinite, others as finite vertically and infinite across; the reasoner concludes it is neither.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha's catalogue of the views of 'some ascetics and brahmins' (DN 1, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: Eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepa) on four grounds: some who do not truly know what is skilful and unskilful refuse to declare anything, (1) from fear and disgust of false speech, (2) from fear and disgust of grasping, since a declaration might arouse desire or aversion, (3) from fear of being cross-examined by clever debaters; (4) one who is dull and stupid, asked about another world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of deeds or the Tathāgata after death, replies 'I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not, nor not not'.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha's catalogue of the views of 'some ascetics and brahmins' (DN 1, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text. The fourth ground repeats verbatim the formula DN 2 gives for Sañjaya; DN 1 names no one.

paraphrase: Fortuitous origination (adhicca-samuppanna) on two grounds: a being fallen from the gods without perception (asaññasatta) recalls in meditation only the arising of perception and concludes 'I did not exist before, now I exist: self and world arose without cause'; the reasoner concludes the same.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha's catalogue of the views of 'some ascetics and brahmins' (DN 1, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: Those who hold the self percipient after death (saññīvāda), on sixteen grounds: it is healthy and percipient after death and is with form, formless, both, neither; finite, infinite, both, neither; of unified perception, of diverse perception, of limited perception, of limitless perception; wholly happy, wholly suffering, both, neither.

paraphrase: Those who hold the self non-percipient after death (asaññīvāda), on eight grounds: with form, formless, both, neither; finite, infinite, both, neither.

paraphrase: Nibbāna here and now (diṭṭhadhamma-nibbānavāda) on five grounds: the self attains supreme nibbāna in this life when it enjoys the five kinds of sense pleasure; others say rather in the first, the second, the third, or the fourth absorption (jhāna).

paraphrase: These sixty-two grounds cover all theories about the past and the future: there is none outside them. The Tathāgata understands them, where they lead, and what is beyond them; not misapprehending, he knows peace within, and having understood the arising, passing, gratification, danger and escape of feelings, is freed by not grasping. The truths he makes known are deep, hard to see, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning (atakkāvacara).
speaker: the Buddha

paraphrase: Every one of these views is only the feeling of those who do not know and see, the agitation of those caught by craving; each is conditioned by contact; without contact they could not be experienced; experienced through the six sense-bases, feeling conditions craving, craving grasping, grasping existence, existence birth, and birth ageing, death and suffering.
speaker: the Buddha
notes: Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: Those views are only the feeling of those who do not know and see, the agitation and writhing of those sunk in craving; they are conditioned by contact, and none of them could be experienced without contact. Those theorists experience them through the six fields of contact, and with feeling as condition comes craving, clinging, becoming, birth, ageing and death. The Tathāgata knows these grounds, their destiny and what lies beyond them, and is freed without clinging.

paraphrase: Those who hold the self neither percipient nor non-percipient after death (nevasaññī-nāsaññīvāda), on the same eight grounds.

paraphrase: All these theorists are caught in this net as the fish of a pond in a fine-meshed net. The Tathāgata's body stands with the cord that leads to becoming cut; while the body lasts gods and humans see him, at its breaking up they will not — as mangoes follow a stalk that is cut.

paraphrase: Annihilationism (ucchedavāda) on seven grounds: the self made of the four great elements and born of mother and father is annihilated at the breaking of the body; others add, in turn, a divine self of the sense-sphere feeding on food, a divine mind-made self complete in all limbs, and selves of the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception — each said to be annihilated at death.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha's catalogue of the views of 'some ascetics and brahmins' (DN 1, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text. The first ground matches the Lokāyata self; the others annihilate 'higher' selves.
